title: feat(v4): add z.isValid and z.isValidAsync
body:
Adds `z.isValid(schema, value)` and `z.isValidAsync(schema, value)`: standalone boolean validation, exported from Zod, Zod Mini, and Zod Core. The return type is a guard on the schema's input type, which stays sound under transforms.

```ts
z.isValid(z.string(), "hi"); // true, and narrows to string
z.isValid(Player, { username: 42 }); // false — no ZodError is ever built
```

On a [compiled schema](https://zod.dev/compile), `isValid` answers directly from the compiled fast path: `compile()` stashes the fast-path function and the runtime fallback on `_zod.bag` (the same caching spot `getDiscriminatedOption` uses), and the fallback call carries the compiler's fallback flag, so user callbacks keep the existing at-most-twice bound on invalid input. The parse module mirrors the compiler's registry sentinels via `Symbol.for` rather than importing it, so nothing new is retained in bundles that don't use it.

The motivation is boolean-only validation on hot paths — accepting or rejecting input without needing the parsed value — which is also the contract of the assert categories in cross-library benchmarks.

Three axes, measured on the moltar fixture with an interleaved min-of-rounds harness (ratios are the meaningful part; the machine was loaded):

| | ops/sec |
| --- | --- |
| `z.isValid`, compiled schema | 45.3M |
| `compiled.safeParse().success` | 52.1M |
| `z.isValid`, uncompiled | 12.5M |
| uncompiled `safeParse().success` | ~9.8M |

An earlier draft stored the fast-path references as properties on the wrapped `run` function; custom properties push function objects into slow storage and it measured 28M. Moving them to the bag recovered fast-mode reads.

Bundle: 0 bytes on every treeshake fixture — the two `Symbol.for` mirrors needed `@__PURE__` annotations, without which the mini fixtures grew 2 gzipped bytes; `bundle-size.test.ts` ceilings are unchanged. Memory: two bag entries on compiled schemas only; `instance-footprint.test.ts` is unchanged.

Docs get a short section under parsing in `basics.mdx`.

inline.body:
`compile()` deliberately keeps async parses off the fast path — `wrapped` bails on `ctx.async` before touching it, and the JSDoc says so. The reason is that `isAsyncFunction` is syntactic, so `.refine((s) => Promise.resolve(...))` compiles fine and the generated code calls `throwAsync()`. Consulting `fastpass` here reintroduces exactly that: `z.isValidAsync(z.compile(schema), "abc")` rejects with `$ZodAsyncError` where both `compiled.safeParseAsync("abc")` and `z.isValidAsync(schema, "abc")` resolve `true`, so merely compiling a schema changes the answer.

<details><summary>Technical details</summary>

````markdown
# `isValidAsync` bypasses the compiler's async guard

## Affected sites
- `packages/zod/src/v4/core/parse.ts:155-159` — the `bag.fastpass && bag.fallbackRun` branch runs the generated fast path even though the caller asked for an async parse.
- `packages/zod/src/v4/core/compile.ts:114-122` — `wrapped` returns `originalRun(payload, ctx)` whenever `ctx.async` is set; `packages/zod/src/v4/core/compile.ts:91-92` documents this as the contract ("Backward (encode), async, and `skipChecks` paths bypass the fast path").
- `packages/zod/src/v4/core/compile.ts:1989` — `isAsyncFunction` only detects syntactically `async` functions, so a plain arrow returning a promise reaches codegen and emits `throwAsync()`.

## Reproduction

```ts
const s = z.string().refine((v) => Promise.resolve(v.length > 1));
const c = z.compile(s);

await z.isValidAsync(s, "abc");        // true
await c.safeParseAsync("abc");         // { success: true }
await z.isValidAsync(c, "abc");        // rejects: $ZodAsyncError
```

Reproduces identically under global mode (`import "zod/compile"`), where the shim populates the same two bag entries.

## Required outcome
- `isValidAsync` must agree with `safeParseAsync` on a compiled schema.
- No test currently covers async on a compiled schema; `is-valid.test.ts:38-44` only exercises the uncompiled path.

## Suggested approach
Drop the fast-path branch from `isValidAsync` and always go through `schema._zod.run`. The compiled wrapper already routes async to the runtime, so nothing is lost — a compiled schema does not get the fast path for `safeParseAsync` today either.
````

</details>

```suggestion
  const ctx: schemas.ParseContextInternal = _ctx ? { ..._ctx, async: true } : { async: true };
  let result: unknown = schema._zod.run({ value, issues: [] }, ctx);
```

`core.input<T>` is a declaration, not something the forward parse enforces, so this predicate can narrow a value to a type it doesn't have. `z.isValid(z.string().catch("x"), 42)` returns `true` and narrows `42` to `string`; same for `z.custom<string>()` and `z.preprocess((v: string) => Number(v), z.number())`. Worth a caveat here and on the `basics.mdx` sentence, which currently states the guarantee unconditionally.

<details><summary>Technical details</summary>

````markdown
# The input-type guard is unsound where `input<T>` is declared rather than validated

## Affected sites
- `packages/zod/src/v4/core/parse.ts:117-121` — `$IsValid` returns `value is core.input<T>` with no caveat.
- `packages/docs/content/basics.mdx:131` — "acts as a type guard on the schema's input type", stated unconditionally.

## Confirmed cases
Each returns `true` at runtime AND narrows statically (verified with `expectTypeOf` under the repo's vitest typecheck project):

| schema | value | `input<T>` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `z.string().catch("x")` | `42` | `string` |
| `z.custom<string>()` | `42` | `string` |
| `z.transform((s: string) => s.length)` | `42` | `string` |
| `z.preprocess((v: string) => Number(v), z.number())` | `42` | `string` |
| `z.string().default("x").nonoptional()` | `undefined` | `string` |
| `z.string().brand<"UserId", "in">()` | `"abc"` | `string & $brand<"UserId">` |

The `transform` case propagates through composition — `z.object({ a: z.transform((s: string) => s.length) })` accepts `{ a: 42 }` and narrows it to `{ a: string }`.

Verified sound (correctly return `false`): `success`, `optional`, `default`/`prefault` alone, `readonly`, `lazy`, `coerce.*`, `instanceof`, `intersection`, `record`, `codec`, `templateLiteral`, `exactOptional`, and `custom` with a predicate.

## Required outcome
- A reader should not come away believing the narrowing is validation-backed for every schema.

## Open questions for the human
- Is a documented caveat enough, or is it worth constraining the predicate? There is no obviously better return type — `catch` and `custom` are genuinely "trust the declaration" schemas — so a note on both the JSDoc and the docs paragraph seems like the proportionate fix. Worth noting this looseness pre-dates the PR; `isValid` is just the first API that turns `input<T>` into a control-flow narrowing, which is what makes it visible.
````

</details>

Addressed in 55bcff0c — verified the new `is-valid.test.ts` assertion fails against the pre-fix code in both the `zod` and `compile-mode` projects.   ｜ [View workflow run](https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/actions/runs/33027456394/job/98372034982) ｜ via [Pullfrog](https://pullfrog.com) ｜ Using `Claude Opus` ｜ [𝕏](https://x.com/pullfrogai)

The comment calls the bag entry `__fastpass`, but line 140 writes `bag.fastpass` — no underscores. The `__` prefix belongs to `__originalRun`, which is a property on the wrapper function rather than on the bag, so the name here doesn't grep to anything.

```suggestion
  // Let later compiles of (or through) this run unwrap to the true runtime — both the global shim and repeated z.compile calls rely on this. The bag's fastpass lets the standalone isValid skip the payload and wrapper on the happy path.
```

Addressed in 9894a31 — the comment now names `bag.fastpass`.   ｜ [View workflow run](https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/actions/runs/33027946343/job/98373588958) ｜ via [Pullfrog](https://pullfrog.com) ｜ Using `Claude Opus` ｜ [𝕏](https://x.com/pullfrogai)

Declining this one. The input type has always trusted the declaration for `catch`, `custom` and `transform`, so the looseness predates this PR, and it's still the right predicate for a guard. Leaving the docs sentence as-is.
